Article https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-65606-1 The Fanconi anemia pathway repairs colibactin-induced DNA interstrand cross-links

Maria Altshuller1, Xu He1, Elliot J. MacKrell1, Kevin M. Wernke2, Yougant Airan 2, Joel W. H. Wong3, Selene Sellés-Baiget4, Ting-Yu Wang5,6, Tsui-Fen Chou 5,6, Julien P. Duxin 4,7, Emily P. Balskus 3,8, Seth B. Herzon 2 & Daniel R. Semlow 1

Colibactin is a secondary metabolite produced by bacteria present in the human gut and is implicated in the development of colorectal cancer. This genotoxin alkylates deoxyadenosines on opposite strands of host cell DNA to produce DNA interstrand cross-links. While cells have evolved multiple mechanisms to resolve (“unhook”) interstrand cross-links, little is known about which of these pathways promote resistance to colibactin. Here, we use Xenopus egg extracts to investigate replication-coupled repair of colibactininduced interstrand cross-links. We show that replication fork stalling at a colibactin-induced interstrand cross-link activates the Fanconi anemia interstrand cross-link repair pathway, which unhooks the interstrand cross-link through nucleolytic incisions. These incisions generate a DNA double-strand break intermediate in one sister chromatid, which can be repaired by homologous recombination, and a monoadduct (“interstrand cross-link remnant”) in the other. Translesion synthesis past the colibactin-induced interstrand cross-link remnant depends on Pol η and the Pol κ-REV1-Pol ζ polymerase complex and introduces predominantly T>A point mutations at the sites of colibactin alkylation. Taken together, our work provides a molecular framework for understanding how cells tolerate a naturally occurring and clinically relevant interstrand cross-link.

Human health is profoundly inﬂuenced by host-microbiome interactions. Emerging data indicate that pathogenic gut bacteria can contribute to dysbiosis and promote inﬂammation by producing toxins that damage host DNA1. pks+ bacteria harbor a 52-kilobase (kb) nonribosomal polypeptide synthetase/polyketide synthase biosynthetic gene cluster that enables production of the colibactin genotoxin2.

Colibactin-producing bacteria are detected in ~40% of patients with inﬂammatory bowel disease and ~60% of patients with colorectal cancer3. Moreover, colibactin exposure is associated with single-base substitution (SBS) and insertion/deletion mutational signatures found in the colonic crypts of most healthy individuals4–6. Colibactin is therefore a highly prevalent and potent driver of human disease.

Colibactin (clb) comprises a pseudo-C2-symmetric scaffold with two cyclopropane groups (Fig. 1a)7–9. Each cyclopropane can react with a deoxyadenosine (dA) to form a monoadduct or a DNA interstrand cross-link (ICL) that covalently links the two DNA strands. Consistently, clb-associated mutational signatures target AT-rich motifs containing offset dAs on opposite strands5,6,10. Once formed, the colibactin-ICL (clb-ICL) renders the alkylated dAs

susceptible to depurination, resulting in an N3 monoalkylated base in one strand and a DNA abasic (AP) site in the other. The AP site can further decompose into a DNA strand break11. Shunt colibactin metabolites that have been isolated from pks+ mutated strains may also alkylate DNA12. Thus, pks+ bacteria likely generate a complicated spectrum of host DNA lesions that mobilize multiple DNA repair pathways.

The clb-ICL is likely to be highly cytotoxic due to its presumed ability to stall replication forks. Failure to repair ICLs encountered during replication can lead to under-replication of the genome and/or gross chromosomal rearrangements. Consequently, cells have evolved multiple repair mechanisms that are activated when a replication fork encounters an ICL (Fig. 1b)13. An ICL induced by acetaldehyde (AA-ICL) can be unhooked through direct reversal of the cross-link14. ICLs formed by psoralen or by AP sites can be unhooked by the NEIL3 DNA glycosylase, which excises a cross-linked base to produce an AP site15. Should these pathways fail, the ICL is unhooked by the Fanconi anemia (FA) pathway13. This pathway is activated when replicative CDC45- MCM2-7-GINS (CMG) helicases stall at an ICL16. CMGs are then polyubiquitylated by the replisome-associated TRAIP E3 ubiquitin ligase, leading to p97-dependent CMG unloading and reversal of one of the two converged forks17–19. At this stage, the FA core complex monoubiquitylates the FANCI-FANCD2 heterodimer, which becomes clamped onto DNA near the ICL20,21. Monoubiquitylated FANCI- FANCD2 recruits structure-speciﬁc nucleases, including XPF-ERCC1, that unhook the ICL through nucleolytic incisions ﬂanking the ICL22. Following restoration of the reversed fork, one sister chromatid contains an ICL remnant that can be bypassed by the REV1-Pol ζ translesion synthesis (TLS) polymerase, while the other chromatid contains a DNA double-strand break (DSB) that is repaired by homologous recombination23,24. Importantly, the FA pathway is thought to be capable of unhooking any ICL, regardless of cross-link structure, and is therefore regarded as the most important pathway for cellular resistance to ICL-inducing agents. Consistent with this inference, mutations in any of 23 genes associated with this pathway cause a human bone marrow failure and cancer predisposition syndrome. Despite the importance of the FA pathway for human health, the physiological ICLs targeted by this pathway remain obscure. Synergy between mutations in the FA pathway and mutations in aldehyde metabolism implies that the FA pathway resolves ICLs formed by endogenous aldehydes, such as formaldehyde or acetaldehyde25,26. Indeed, a chemically synthesized acetaldehyde-ICL is processed by the FA pathway in Xenopus egg extracts14. However, ICLs induced by acetaldehyde or any other endogenous metabolite have not been conﬁrmed in vivo. Furthermore, FANC proteins have been shown to promote a variety of genome maintenance mechanisms in addition to ICL repair, including homologous recombination, replication fork protection, R-loop resolution, retrotransposon suppression, and mitochondrial genome maintenance27–31. Intriguingly, indirect evidence suggests that colibactin-induced ICLs might be repaired by the FA pathway. Colibactin exposure induces FANCD2 ubiquitylation and FANCD2 foci formation in cells, and FANCD2-deﬁcient cells are hypersensitive to colibactin32. However, given the spectrum of DNA lesions produced during colibactin exposure and the multiple genoprotective functions of FANCD2, it remains unclear whether colibactininduced ICLs are repaired by the FA pathway.

Here, we use Xenopus egg extracts to investigate replicationcoupled repair of site-speciﬁc ICLs formed by either the native colibactin toxin or a synthetic colibactin analog. We ﬁnd that both ICLs are strong impediments to DNA replication that trigger replicationcoupled repair by the FA pathway. TLS past both an unhooked colibactin-induced ICL remnant and a colibactin monoadduct requires REV1 and Pol κ. We further show that colibactin-induced ICL repair can be error-free but frequently introduces primarily T>A point mutations. These results deﬁne the mechanisms that allow cells to tolerate a DNA lesion that may drive the development of CRC and demonstrate the FA pathway’s capacity to repair physiologically relevant ICLs.

Results Colibactin-induced ICL repair is coupled to DNA replication To investigate colibactin-induced ICL repair in Xenopus egg extracts, we prepared plasmids containing site-speciﬁc ICLs generated with either native colibactin (clb) or a synthetic colibactin analog (c742; Fig. 1a). c742 contains an unsubstituted carbon-carbon linker in place of a central diketone that is susceptible to oxidative cleavage. The stabilized analog produces an ICL that is otherwise structurally identical to a clb-ICL and that can induce cell cycle arrest in human cells33. Short oligonucleotide duplexes containing a colibactin alkylation motif were incubated with either c742 or with cultured pks+ bacteria. In both cases, cross-links were expected to form between dAs at the second position of a palindromic 5′-AATATT-3′ target sequence (Supplementary Fig. 1a)5,6. Following puriﬁcation, essentially all the duplexes contained a colibactin-induced ICL (Supplementary Fig. 1b); these were then ligated into ~5.6 kb plasmids. At least 75% of the puriﬁed c742-ICL plasmid (pICLc742) contained an intact ICL (Supplementary Fig. 1c). However, only ~50% of the clb-ICL plasmid (pICLclb) contained an intact ICL (Supplementary Fig. 1c), despite preparing the plasmids using highly puriﬁed cross-linked oligonucleotides (Supplementary Fig. 1b). Interestingly, a substantial fraction of the pICLclb plasmids contained AP sites and monoadducts, presumably consisting of clb linked to adenine (clb-A) (Supplementary Fig. 1d, e), which indicates that the clb-ICL can undergo depurination during plasmid preparation. Consistent with previous work, the AP sites in our pICLclb preparations are rapidly removed in egg extracts (Supplementary Fig. 1f)34. We therefore infer that replication forks encounter either a clb- ICL or a clb-A monoadduct, but not an AP site, during pICLclb replication in egg extracts. Initially, the plasmids were detected as X-shaped structures that migrate slowly due to the presence of a cross-link. Replication intermediates were then resolved on a native agarose gel and visualized by autoradiography (Fig. 1d). For comparison, we also replicated an undamaged plasmid (pCtrl) and plasmids containing either a cisplatin-ICL (pICLPt) or an AP-ICL (pICLAP). Whereas replicated pCtrl rapidly accumulated as open circular and supercoiled products, each of the ICL-containing plasmids initially accumulated as slowly migrating “ﬁgure 8” intermediates that form when CMG helicases converge and stall on either side of the ICL. In the case of pICLAP, the slow ﬁgure 8s were rapidly converted into open circular and supercoiled products, indicative of unhooking by the NEIL3 glycosylase15. In the case of pICLc742 and pICLclb, the slow ﬁgure 8s were ﬁrst converted into a series of species with intermediate mobilities and later into open circular and supercoiled products. Note that pICLclb*

replication resulted in substantial accumulation of open circular and supercoiled plasmids at even early time points, consistent with the presence of uncross-linked plasmid in this preparation. Interestingly, pICLc742 and pICLclb replication produced intermediates that closely resembled those formed during replication of pICLPt, which is repaired by the FA pathway in egg extracts36,37. These ﬁndings indicate that colibactin-induced ICLs block replication fork progression and activate repair. In egg extracts, the convergence of replication forks at the ICL triggers TRAIP-dependent polyubiquitylation of CMG17. Short ubiquitin chains on CMG are sufﬁcient to recruit the NEIL3 glycosylase, while longer chains enable p97-dependent CMG unloading and activation of the FA pathway. We conﬁrmed that colibactin-induced ICL repair requires fork convergence (Supplementary Fig. 1i) and so tested whether it also requires CMG unloading. Addition of p97 inhibitor (NMS-87338) to pICLc742 and pICLclb replication reactions caused a persistence of slow ﬁgure 8s and a reduction in unhooked open circular and supercoiled products (Fig. 1e), indicating that repair is activated by CMG unloading. Importantly, the absence of unhooking in p97- inhibited extracts implies that c742- and clb-ICLs are not processed by the NEIL3 or AA-ICL pathways, which do not require CMG unloading14,15. We additionally conﬁrmed that depletion of NEIL3 from extracts has a negligible effect on the repair of pICLc742 (Supplementary Fig. 1j, k). We also examined the effect of p97 inhibition on maturation of nascent DNA strands by digesting repair intermediates with restriction enzymes (AﬂIII and EcoRI) that enable resolution of nascent leading strands on a denaturing sequencing gel (Fig. 1f).During pICLc742

and pICLclb replication, the nascent leading strands initially stall ~20 to 40 nucleotides (nt) upstream of the ICL due to the footprint of CMG. They are subsequently extended to 1 nt upstream of the expected dA cross-link positions before eventually being converted into full-length extension products. Consistent with a requirement for CMG unloading during pICLc742 and pICLclb repair, p97 inhibitor attenuated extension of the nascent strands from the −20 to −40 stall positions to the −1 position and suppressed the formation of extension products. Note that the effect on extension product accumulation is more pronounced for pICLc742 than for pICLclb, consistent with the presence of uncross-linked plasmid in the pICLclb preparation. We conclude that colibactin-induced ICL repair is activated by fork convergence and CMG unloading, suggestive of FA pathway repair. We noticed that replication of pICLc742 consistently produced two prominent intermediates that were not observed during replication of

pICLAP, pICLPt, or pICLclb (e.g., Fig. 1d, e, red arrowheads). Our characterizations of these intermediates indicate that both species accumulate after CMG unloading and approach of the nascent leading strands up to the ICL (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Fig. 1h; see below). We suspect that these intermediates correspond to topological isomers of cross-linked fast ﬁgure 8 structures that have undergone CMG unloading but not fork reversal. It is possible that the structure of the c742-ICL might somehow antagonize fork reversal, though additional studies will be required to conﬁrm this hypothesis.

FA pathway proteins are recruited to colibactin-induced ICLs during replication To determine which repair networks are activated during colibactininduced ICL repair, we performed unbiased quantitative mass spectrometry on chromatin recovered from pICLc742 replication reactions (Supplementary Fig. 2a, b)39,40. As expected, we observed that the CMG helicase, Pol δ, Pol ε, and other replisome components were enriched on pICLc742 at early replication time points (Fig. 2a). Replisome recruitment was inhibited by geminin, which blocks helicase loading (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 2c)41. Replisome components decreased in abundance over time, consistent with both replication termination and replisome disassembly following fork convergence at the ICL (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 2d). Replisome dissociation from pICLc742 coincided with recruitment of proteins that participate in the FA pathway, including ATR-ATRIP, FANCI-FANCD2, structurespeciﬁc nuclease complexes, TLS polymerases, and homologous recombination proteins (Fig. 2a). Importantly, FA pathway proteins were enriched on pICLc742 relative to both pCtrl and pICLc742 that was incubated in egg extract supplemented with geminin, indicating that these repair factors are recruited in a damage- and replicationdependent manner (Fig. 2b, c). Surprisingly, FANCM and the FA core complex were most abundant on pCtrl (at both 10 and 90 min after replication initiation) and on pICLc742 that was incubated in gemininsupplemented extract (Fig. 2a). These factors were similarly abundant during the ﬁrst 30 min of pICLc742 replication. Despite the puzzling recruitment dynamics of the FA core complex, we nonetheless observed that replication of pICLc742 and pICLclb, but not pCtrl, stimulated monoubiquitylation of FANCD2 in egg extracts (Fig. 2d) and that this ubiquitylation was temporally correlated with recruitment of FANCI-FANCD2 to chromatin (Fig. 2a). Taken together, these data indicate that the FA pathway is mobilized during replication-coupled repair of colibactin-induced ICLs.

Colibactin-induced ICLs are unhooked by the FA pathway ICL repair by the FA pathway involves nucleolytic incisions that effectively convert the ICL into a DSB. Replication of pICLc742 resulted in the transient accumulation of DNA fragments consistent with DSB formation during nucleolytic repair (Supplementary Fig. 3a). This accumulation of putative pICLc742 incision products closely mirrored the accumulation of established FA pathway pICLPt incision products36,37. By contrast, incision products did not appreciably accumulate during replication of pICLAP, which is predominantly unhooked without incisions by NEIL315. Over time, the incision products disappeared, presumably due to DSB repair by homologous recombination factors, which our data indicate are recruited to plasmids containing a colibactin-induced ICL (Fig. 2). To explicitly test whether replication-coupled repair of colibactininduced ICLs requires the FA pathway, we replicated pICLc742 and pICLclb in mock- or FANCD2-immunodepleted extracts supplemented with recombinant (r)FANCI-FANCD2, as indicated (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Fig. 3b, c). Native agarose gel analysis of replication intermediates revealed that FANCD2 depletion resulted in an accumulation of reversed fork intermediates and concomitant reductions in unhooked open circular and supercoiled plasmids (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Fig. 3d), indicating a defect in ICL repair. TLS during colibactin-induced ICL repair depends on REV1, Pol κ, and Pol η Following ICL unhooking, TLS extends the nascent DNA strands past damaged nucleotides in the template DNA strands. For ICLs formed by nitrogen mustard and cisplatin, TLS is mediated by an insertion polymerase, which inserts a nucleotide opposite the damaged base, and the REV1-Pol ζ complex, which extends the DNA strand23. In contrast, REV1 is required for both insertion and extension during repair of ICLs formed by acetaldehyde, psoralen, or AP sites14,15. REV1 immunodepletion largely abolished the formation of supercoiled plasmids during pICLc742 replication (Fig. 4a, b). This was accompanied by an accumulation of open circular plasmids, indicating a requirement for REV1 during TLS past the unhooked c742-ICL remnant. REV1 depletion also caused a pronounced accumulation of open circular plasmids during pICLclb replication (Fig. 4b), indicating that bypass of either an unhooked clb-ICL remnant or a clb-A monoadduct also depends on REV1 (see below). Supercoiled plasmid still accumulated during pICLclb

replication in REV1-depleted extract, likely due to repair of template strand AP sites produced upon clb-ICL depurination (Supplementary Fig. 1f). For both pICLc742 and pICLclb, REV1 depletion caused a strong reduction in nascent strand extension products and a persistence of −1 stall products (Fig. 4c, d and Supplementary Fig. 4a), distinct from the persistence of insertion (0 stall position) products observed during cisplatin-ICL repair in REV1-depleted extracts (Supplementary Fig. 4b–d)23. Our data, therefore, indicate that REV1 is required for both insertion and extension during TLS past a colibactin-induced ICL remnant. In some experiments, small amounts of insertion products were detected during repair of the c742-ICL that were suppressed by REV1 depletion (e.g., Supplementary Fig. 4d). We tested whether Pol κ also promotes TLS during repair of pICLc742. Like REV1 immunodepletion, Pol κ immunodepletion

strongly inhibited the formation of supercoiled plasmids and caused a corresponding accumulation of open circular plasmid, consistent with defective TLS (Fig. 4e–g). For example, in previous work, the Pol κ antibody used in our experiments co-depleted the FA core complex, which has been implicated in TLS regulation42,43. In cells and organoids, colibactin exposure is associated primarily with T>C SBSs, and less frequently with T>A and T>G SBSs. Interestingly, c742-ICL repair produced mostly T>A SBSs, with fewer T>G and T>C SBSs. This suggests that while the FA pathway may account for colibactin-induced T>A mutations, another mutagenic process may generate T>C mutations associated with colibactin exposure. Essentially, no insertion mutations were observed. The majority of deletion mutations (90.1%) at least partially overlapped the 4-bp region spanned by the cross-link. FANCD2 depletion resulted in a dramatic increase in the proportion of plasmid sequences containing deletion mutations (45.7%; Fig. 6b, right). In the absence of the FA pathway, stalled replication forks may undergo aberrant fork cleavage and subsequent end-joining, resulting in the formation of deletions. We next tested whether REV1 or Pol κ inﬂuences the spectrum of mutations observed following pICLc742 replication in egg extract. pICLc742 was replicated in mock-, REV1-, or Pol κ-depleted egg extract, and the repair products were sequenced (Supplementary Fig. 7a–f). Replication in mock-depleted extract produced 39.3% error-free repair products and 38.9% SBS repair products (Fig. 7a, left). By contrast, REV1 depletion reduced the proportion of plasmid sequences that were free of mutations or contained SBSs (26.4% error-free and 9.7% SBSs; Fig. 7a, right), as did Pol κ depletion (32.4% error-free and 4.6% SBSs; Fig. 7a, center). Taken together, these results indicate that REV1 and Pol κ act in concert during mutagenic bypass of an unhooked

colibactin-induced ICL. Notably, although the frequency of SBSs decreased upon REV1 or Pol κ depletion, the relative distribution of T>A, T>G, and T>C mutations was similar across mock-, REV1-, and Pol κ-depleted extracts (Fig. 7b), suggesting that residual REV1 and Pol κ mediate bypass of the ICL remnant in the depleted extracts. Strikingly, REV1 and Pol κ depletion increased both the frequency and size of deletion mutations present in the recovered replication products: the frequency of reads containing deletions increased from 20.8% in mock-depleted extract to 61.5% in both REV1- and Pol κ-depleted extracts (Fig. 7a, c). These results suggest that an alternative deletionprone mechanism can bypass colibactin-induced ICLs in the absence of REV1- and Pol κ-dependent TLS. Since most fully replicated pICLclb plasmids were generated upon replication of contaminating uncross-linked plasmids (Supplementary Fig. 1c–e), we were unable to distinguish the mutation spectrum produced during clb-ICL repair. Instead, we examined the mutagenicity of a colibactin-induced monoadduct. We replicated pICLclb in mock-, REV1-, or Pol κ-depleted egg extract supplemented with p97 inhibitor (to once again inactivate ICL repair by the FA pathway) and sequenced the replication products (Fig. 7d and Supplementary Fig. 7g–l). Replication past clb-A monoadducts in mock-depleted extract produced a mutation spectrum mirroring that produced during c742-ICL repair. Error-free bypass was observed in 64.4% of the plasmid sequences, while SBSs were present in 16.8% of the plasmids sequences (Fig. 7e). Again, we observed predominantly T>A SBSs at the colibactin hotspot with smaller frequencies of T>G and T>C mutations (Fig. 7f). Depletion of either REV1 or Pol κ dramatically reduced the frequency of SBSs (5.8% and 3.0% for REV1 and Pol κ depletion, respectively; Fig. 7e, f), indicating that REV1- and Pol κ-dependent TLS is responsible for the spectrum of point mutations observed upon bypass of a colibactininduced monoadduct. REV1 and Pol κ depletions also resulted in a higher frequency of deletion mutations (14.5% in mock-depleted extract, compared with 23.6% in REV1-depleted extract and 46.7% in Pol κ-depleted; Fig. 7e). This increase in deletion frequency was accompanied by a shift toward longer deletions (Fig. 7g). These trends were consistent across independent experimental replicates (Supplementary Fig. 7d–f, j–l). Thus, although REV1- and Pol κ-dependent TLS past a clb-A adduct introduces frequent point mutations, it appears to suppress an alternative bypass mechanism that is prone to larger deletions. Combined, our sequencing data indicate that REV1- and Pol κ-dependent TLS promotes mutagenic bypass of both unhooked colibactin-induced ICL remnants and colibactin-induced monoadducts.

Discussion Despite intense interest in colibactin as a driver of colorectal cancer, little is known about the pathways that repair colibactin-induced DNA damage. Our data indicate that colibactin-induced ICL repair is activated upon convergence of replication forks at the lesion and unloading of the replisome (Fig. 8a). The FA pathway then mediates nucleolytic incisions that release the cross-link and generate a DSB, which is likely repaired by homologous recombination, and an ICL remnant, which is bypassed by TLS. Mutations in the FA pathway strongly synergize with mutations in ALDH2 and ADH5, which enable detoxiﬁcation of acetaldehyde and formaldehyde, respectively25,26, implying that unrepaired ICLs produced by endogenous reactive aldehydes cause FA. However, the speciﬁc chemical structures of aldehyde-induced ICLs that arise in human cells and drive progression of FA remain elusive. To our knowledge, the clb-ICL is the only naturally occurring ICL with both genetic and physical evidence to substantiate its formation in vivo3–8. Our data therefore demonstrate that the FA pathway repairs an ICL that is likely to arise at some point over the lifetime of most individuals. While our data reveal that the FA pathway promotes resistance to colibactin-induced ICLs, it is unclear whether colibactin contributes to the etiology or progression of FA. We are unaware of any evidence linking pks+ bacteria to bone marrow failure, and current data do not suggest that FA patients are at elevated risk for CRC, though sporadic cases have been reported46. Interestingly, the colibactin-associated mutational signature has been detected in squamous cell carcinomas, a cancer for which FA patients are at dramatically increased risk47. A recent genomic analysis of squamous cell carcinomas from FA patients did not identify colibactin-associated SBSs or single-nucleotide deletions48. However, it may be that colibactin-induced DNA damage manifests different mutational signatures in individuals lacking a functional FA pathway. In FA patients, colibactin exposure may instead produce more complex structural variants at AT-rich colibactin alkylation hotspots due to alternative processing of ICLs. The colibactinassociated mutational signature has also been detected in cancers derived from additional tissue types47. Future studies are therefore warranted to determine whether FA patients are at increased risk for complications arising due to colonization by pks+ bacteria. Colibactin exhibits a striking speciﬁcity for the N3 position of dA in AT-rich motifs10. The three-dimensional structure of a colibactininduced ICL implicates hydrogen bonding and electrostatic interactions within the relatively narrow minor groove of AT-rich DNA in the speciﬁcity of colibactin-ICL formation10. Both monoalkylation by colibactin and nucleolytic unhooking of a colibactin-induced ICL generate similar adducts comprising an N3 alkylated dA (in the latter case, the colibactin scaffold may be further linked to the short oligonucleotide generated by unhooking incisions). In general, TLS past minor groove adducts is thought to depend primarily on the polymerase activity of Pol κ. Pol κ-deﬁcient cells are hypersensitive to genotoxins that induce minor groove adducts (e.g., illudin S and mitomycin C), and Pol κ has been shown to efﬁciently extend DNA primers past N2-dG adducts (e.g., benzo[a]pyrene-N2-dG) and N3-dA adducts (e.g., 3-deaza-3-methyl-dA) in vitro49,50. Additionally, TLS past a p3d-Phen-A adduct in egg extract was recently reported to depend on Pol κ polymerase activity, but not on REV142. It is therefore somewhat surprising that the bypass of colibactin-induced adducts requires REV1 but not Pol κ polymerase activity. Despite having a catalytically active site that can accommodate minor groove adducts51, Pol κ might be inhibited by the much larger size of the colibactin adducts (clb-A molecular weight is

~900 Da). Colibactin may also make additional contacts to DNA in the minor groove that impede insertion by Pol κ. Finally, we note that previous studies have examined bypass of N3-dA adducts using stabilizing 3-deaza-substituted dA analogs that may not completely recapitulate the effects of N3 alkylation42. Our data also indicate that Pol η promotes the approach of nascent leading strands to within 1 nt of a colibactin-induced ICL. Based on the timing of the nascent strand approach, we infer that Pol η helps to extend the nascent strands after CMG unloading and before FANCI- FANCD2-dependent incisions unhook the ICL. REV1 and Pol κ then act together to enable insertion opposite the alkylated base and subsequent extension past the lesion. Similar coordination between Pol η and REV1-Pol ζ has been observed during bypass of DNA-protein crosslinks, cisplatin-induced intrastrand cross-links, and UV-induced 6,4 photoproducts52–54. In thesecases, Pol η normally performs insertionof a nucleotide opposite the lesion while REV1-Pol ζ performs the extension step. In the case of colibactin-ICLs, however, Pol η appears unable to perform insertion, even when REV1 is absent. It may be that the structure of the colibactin-ICL blocks insertion by Pol η. In the context of model ICL duplexes, strand displacement synthesis and insertion by Pol η was shown to be inhibited by a non-distorting ICL, resulting in an accumulation of −1 stall products55. The relatively nondistorting colibactin-ICL may also suppress insertion by Pol η, necessitating insertion by Pol κ-REV1-Pol ζ once unhooking has occurred10. Mutational signatures associated with colibactin exposure include predominantly T>C SBSs at AT-rich hexanucleotide sequences and single-nucleotide T deletions at T-homopolymer sequences4–6. T>G and T>A SBSs are also detected, though less frequently than T>C mutations. Our data provide some insight as to the origin of these mutational signatures. Bypass of both unhooked colibactin-induced ICL remnants and monoadducts can introduce a T>A point mutation through the insertion of dA opposite an alkylated dA. This immediately suggests that the T>A mutations observed in cells, organoids, and colonic crypts exposed to colibactin arise through Pol κ-REV1-Pol ζ- dependent TLS past colibactin adducts. This subset of colibactinassociated SBSs may therefore represent a mutational signature for clb-ICL repair by the FA pathway. How then might the more prevalent T>C mutations arise? A trivial explanation is that Pol κ-REV1-Pol ζ-dependent TLS past a colibactin adduct produces different mutations in frogs and humans due to divergence of the TLS polymerases between species. Alternatively, T>C mutations might be produced through distinct ICL repair mechanisms or through repair of distinct colibactin-induced DNA lesions. ICLs can be unhooked through replication-independent mechanisms involving mismatch repair or transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair45,56. Both pathways would generate a ssDNA gap at the lesion and require TLS past an ICL remnant in the remaining strand. Interestingly, the catalytic activity of Pol κ is required for replication-independent ICL repair45. Colibactin-induced ICLs can decompose into DSBs through depurination and AP site cleavage, requiring DNA end-joining. Preparation of Xenopus egg extracts Preparation of high-speed supernatant (HSS) and nucleoplasmic extracts (NPE) from Xenopus laevis eggs was performed as described previously60. Brieﬂy, HSS was prepared from eggs collected from six laboratory-bred wild-type adult female X. laevis (aged >2 years). Eggs were dejellied in 1 L of 2.2% (w/v) cysteine, pH 7.7, washed with 2 L 0.5X Marc’s Modiﬁed Ringer’s solution (2.5 mM HEPES-KOH [pH 7.8], 50 mM NaCl, 1 mM KCl, 0.25 mM MgSO4, 1.25 mM CaCl2, 0.05 mM EDTA), and washed with 1 L of Egg Lysis Buffer (ELB) (10 mM HEPES- KOH [pH 7.7], 50 mM KCl, 2.5 mM MgCl2, 250 mM sucrose, 1 mM dithiothreitol [DTT], and 50 μg mL cycloheximide). Eggs were then packed in 14-mL round-bottom Falcon tubes at 200 × g using a Sorvall ST8 swinging bucket rotor. Eggs were supplemented with 5 μg mL−1

aprotinin, 5 μg mL−1 leupeptin, and 2.5 μg mL−1 cytochalasin B and then crushed by centrifugation at 20,000 × g for 20 min at 4 °C in a TH13- 6×50 rotor using a Sorvall Lynx 4000 centrifuge. The low-speed supernatant (LSS) was collected by removing the soluble extract layer and supplemented with 50 μg mL−1 cycloheximide, 1 mM DTT, 10 μg mL−1 aprotinin, 10 μg mL−1 leupeptin, and 5 μg mL−1 cytochalasin B. This extract was then spun in thin-walled ultracentrifuge tubes at 260,000 × g for 90 min at 2 °C in a TLS-55 rotor using a tabletop ultracentrifuge. Lipids were aspirated off the top layer, and HSS was harvested, aliquoted, snap frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at −80 °C. NPE preparation also began with extracting LSS, except eggs were collected from 20 laboratory-bred wild-type female X. laevis (aged >2 years), and the volumes used to dejelly and wash the eggs were doubled (2 L of 2.2% cysteine, 4 L of 0.5X Marc’s Modiﬁed Ringer’s solution, and 2 L of ELB). LSS was supplemented with 50 μg mL−1

cycloheximide, 1 mM DTT, 10 µg mL−1 aprotinin, 10 µg mL−1 leupeptin, 5 µg mL−1 cytochalasin B, and 3.3 μg mL−1 nocodazole. The LSS was then spun at 20,000 × g for 15 min at 4 °C in a TH13-6×50 rotor using a Sorvall Lynx 4000 centrifuge. The top lipid layer was removed, and the cytoplasm was transferred to a 50-mL conical tube. ATP regenerating mix (2 mM ATP, 20 mM phosphocreatine, and 5 μg mL−1 creatine phosphokinase) was added to the extract. Preparation of next-generation sequencing libraries In preparation for NGS, plasmids were replicated as described above. After extraction and ethanol precipitation, samples were resuspended to a concentration of approximately 10–15 ng µL−1. Four microliters of recovered DNA were mixed with 200 nM each of forward and reverse primer (see Supplementary Table 1), 200 µM dNTPs, and 2 units of Phusion High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase (NEB) in 1X Phusion HF buffer to a total volume of 100 µL. Amplicons were generated by PCR with initial heating to 98 °C for 30 s, followed by 18 cycles of 98 °C for 10 s, 55 °C for 30 s, and 72 °C for 30 s, and a ﬁnal incubation at 72 °C for 10 min. The ampliﬁed DNA was puriﬁed with a QIAquick PCR Puriﬁcation Kit (Qiagen) per the manufacturer’s instructions and inspected on a 0.8% agarose, 1X TBE gel visualized with SYBR Gold to conﬁrm ampliﬁcation. Samples were then submitted to Azenta for paired-end NGS (Illumina MiSeq, 2 × 250 bp).

NGS data processing Raw sequencing reads were cropped to 150 bp using Trimmomatic (v0.39) to avoid later merging failures due to sequencing errors at the ends of amplicons70. Reads were then processed using SIQ (v1.8) with long-read analysis enabled and otherwise default settings, and the SIQPlotteR web tool was used to generate plots71. pICLclb contains a single C-C mismatch designed to distinguish reads derived from the two parental strands. These were not deconvoluted in our analysis;

instead, the SBS corresponding to the C-C mismatch was manually removed from the SIQ output for pICLclb data sets.
